title: What counts as straight? (worked out on cardboard)
note: The authored thinking for one hall, in the first person, by the pass (Claude), for Palle's request of 2026-11-14 (see Russell_Paradox.json). 'at' is the floor's own frame in metres (x east, z south), 'yaw' in degrees. A sticker of kind 'quote' stands word for word in the hall text; every other kind is mine and may be wrong - the plates say where I am unsure.

hero.why: The bench is where the hall's question is asked: one record of three corners and a slider with three stops - DISK, PLANE, SPHERE - that changes what a side is. The dome in the middle of the floor is its SPHERE stop made walkable, not a second hero.
hero.staging: The bench stood at [-3, 10], a metre beyond the slab's south edge, in the air where nobody could reach it (the tower validator: 'leaves the structural floor'). The pass moved it onto the slab at the visitor's left hand on arrival, with a ring of tape and one work light; plate 1 stands at the right hand, and the threads run north across the floor from the dome to the disk and the surfaces.

plates.title: 1  WHAT COUNTS AS STRAIGHT
front: The triangle did not change. I changed what a side is.
On the plane a side is the straight segment between two corners.
On the sphere that segment would dive through the inside. So a side is the shortest way that STAYS ON the surface.
'Straight' was never one thing. It means: shortest, among the paths this space allows.
I had been treating the plane's answer as the meaning of the word.
back: the bench is on your left as you land: one slider, three stops - DISK, PLANE, SPHERE. this cardboard is about what the slider changes.

plates.title: 2  THE SAME THREE PAIRS, READ TWICE
front: Three pairs of numbers. On the plane they place points. On the sphere they name directions from the centre.
What travels: the record. What does not: distances, angles, the sum.
On the dome I measured 183 on top and 190 two metres out. On the mat: 180, every time.
The excess grows with the ground the triangle encloses.
So the sum was never a fact about triangles. It was a fact about where they live.
back: on a sphere: (sum - 180, in radians) = area / R x R. the dome's R is 6 m.
my 190 triangle should then enclose about 6.3 square metres. plausible. somebody pace it out.

plates.title: 3  THE SHORTER WAY THAT LEFT
front: A plank goes through the dome from cone to cone.
It is shorter than the red line on the surface. It is not a side of the triangle.
'Shorter' is only a complaint if I forget which space the corners belong to.
First say where you are. Then ask what is straight.
(Russell, one floor down, did the same thing to 'everything': say within what, then ask.)
back: a tunnel is a fine way to travel. it is just not geometry ON the sphere.

plates.title: 4  A RIM YOU CANNOT REACH
front: The disk lies flat on its stand and stands for a space whose rim is infinitely far away.
A step near the rim counts for more than a step in the middle.
So the picture's size is not the space's size, and its curved lines are that space's straight ones.
The picture ends. The thing it shows does not.
I keep mistaking the edge of a drawing for the edge of the world. This object is built to catch me at it.
back: angles in the disk are true. lengths are not. a map can keep one honesty and give up another.
which honesty did my dome keep? both - on a sphere you can. (plate 6)

plates.title: 5  A BEND IS NOT A METRIC
front: Saddle, dome, slider. I see a bend and think I am seeing the geometry.
A bend in my room is a shape IN flat space. A metric is a rule for distance.
Roll a flat sheet into a tube: it is bent, and its triangles still add to 180.
So the silhouette proves nothing. The triangle's sum does.
The slider changes its own sketch. It does not govern the room.
back: test for any curved thing here: draw a triangle ON it and add the corners. do not judge it from the side.

plates.title: 6  THE FLOOR STAYED FLAT. THEN I BUILT A DOME
front: The hall says the benches do not bend the museum: we walk between them on the same ordinary floor.
Then I put a dome on that floor and let you be a corner. Is that cheating?
No - but it is luck. A dome is bent in the room AND round in its distances. On a sphere the two agree.
For the disk they cannot: nothing I could build in this room has the disk's distances everywhere.
So one of the three geometries can be walked here, and one can only be pictured.
back: I think that last claim is Hilbert's theorem (no complete surface of constant negative curvature in ordinary space). I have not checked the statement. a saddle has it in a patch only.
the wing behind the door on the south edge does picture them and lets you travel in the picture. its own first note: 'Physical support stays Euclidean.'

plates.title: 7  WHICH ONE IS THE WORLD?
front: Three geometries, each consistent. Mathematics allows all of them.
Which one the world has is not decided by the triangle on the bench.
That needs a measurement of the world: a triangle big enough, and corners I trust.
This is the first of the three edges: a CHOICE. Nothing broke.
Next floor a rule does break. Keep the difference.
back: Gauss is said to have measured a triangle between three mountain tops. I have not checked the story.

plates.title: 8  A DOOR IS NOT A CURVATURE
front: Behind this door stand seven rooms that are not behind this door. Look past the frame: sky.
The first is bigger than its doorway allows. Every tile of its floor is an ordinary flat tile.
So nothing in there is bent. What changed is which piece of floor is next to which.
Three different things are called non-Euclidean on this floor: a bent surface (the dome), a rule for distance (the disk), a gluing (this door).
A gluing leaves every triangle at 180 - unless the triangle goes round a seam that turns you.
back: room 3 in there carries an arrow round three right angles and it comes back turned. that one IS curvature. a door that only moves you is not.
the last line on the front is my understanding, not checked: a seam that turns you is a cone point, and a triangle round it gains or loses exactly that turn.

threads.why: If straight depends on the space, the same record can be read in two spaces and give two sums.

threads.word: what a side may not do
threads.why: The record travels; the chord shows what does not: a side must stay in the space.
The plank is shorter and is not straight here, because it is not among the allowed paths.
The disk is a third interpretation of a retained record: angles kept, lengths not.
The disk looks flat and is not; the saddle looks curved and that proves nothing. Both say: do not judge from outside.
On a sphere the bend in the room and the rule for distance happen to agree, which is why a dome can be walked.
The disk's distances cannot be had on any whole surface in this room; it stays a picture.
Less than, equal to, more than 180: three readings, each consistent.
Being able to walk one geometry here does not make it the world's.
Which space the corners belong to is the question the world has to answer, not the bench.

threads.word: a gluing is not a bend
threads.why: The saddle is bent and proves nothing; the door bends nothing and still gives a room that will not fit.
What counts as straight depends on the space; the door changes the space by changing what is next to what.

visual_arguments.title: THE WALKED TRIANGLE
visual_arguments.claim: The same three corners have a different angle sum on a surface whose straightest paths are not the plane's.
visual_arguments.from_the_hall: The bench's PLANE and SPHERE, and the tutorial's record of three coordinate pairs read twice.
built_from: a walkable cap of a sphere (a mesh of its own)
trace_point_ball (the three points on the mat)
visual_arguments.what_stands: A dome 6.4 m across with two cones and a plank through it; north of it a mat with the same three pairs read as a plane.
visual_arguments.what_you_do: Step onto the dome: you are the third corner. Walk away from the cones and read the sum on the board; the mat keeps 180.
visual_arguments.what_it_shows: The sum is a fact about the space the corners belong to. The record travels between the two readings; the angles do not.

visual_arguments.status: standing: row f2_noneuclidean_wing_13_4 (not the pass's work: commons/artifacts/noneuclidean_wing with its Void adapter; the pass moved it clear of a column)
visual_arguments.title: SEVEN SPACES
visual_arguments.claim: A door can lead to more room than there is behind it, and a room can be flat, round or hyperbolic while the deck you stand on stays ordinary.
visual_arguments.from_the_hall: The hall's own installed wing. Its door is a stencil doorway (Godot 4.5's stencil buffer): a quad writes stencil 5, a copy of the first room is drawn only where stencil is 5.
built_from: a door frame on the slab
seven chambers 60 m above it and five more spaces behind two doors in the first (overlapping rooms, a growing corner walk, a forced perspective, a repeating gallery, a column forest, a labyrinth)
visual_arguments.what_stands: A dark frame on the south edge with a carried point on a pedestal beside it. From the side: sky behind it. From the front: a room.
visual_arguments.what_you_do: Walk through. Next / Previous / Museum on the desk in each chamber; the point is carried through every room.
visual_arguments.what_it_shows: 1 a room that will not fit, 2 a corridor that returns your point, 3 an arrow that does not return (three right angles), 4 the disk's edge, 5 hyperbolic galleries H2 x R, 6 H3, 7 a straight aim and a curved path.
visual_arguments.measured: tools/probes/noneuclid_wing_visit.gd: at [-5, 8] a column stood 0.55 m in front of the door and the tower's walker never got in; at [-9.5, 8] it enters, stands in each of the seven chambers and returns (4 of 4).

visual_arguments.title: THREE CORNERS AND YOU ARE HOME
visual_arguments.claim: A walk with three right-angled corners can close on a floor that is flat under every step, if all the curvature sits at one point inside the block you walk round.
visual_arguments.from_the_hall: The bench's SPHERE triangle with three right angles, and room 3 of the wing ('Three right angles. The same position; a different direction.').
built_from: a closed cardboard corridor round a square block, four sides built alike, one door with a paper screen
a number on each face of the block, lettered from where the body stands
visual_arguments.what_stands: A cardboard block 4.8 m square on the west wing beside the standing 180, with '3 corners / IN' on its door and a board beside it.
visual_arguments.what_you_do: Go in, keep the block on your left, count the corners. After three you stand at 1 and the door again, and leave by the door you came in by.
visual_arguments.what_it_shows: 270 on flat floor: the dome's excess gathered into one point (a cube's corner, laid out). The same work with `corners` five closes after five (450: the disk's surplus at one point), with four it is an ordinary block.
visual_arguments.how: The inside has three quarter-sectors, the building four. The body is turned about the block's middle by a quarter when it steps onto a side the glued space does not have, in the frame the faces are re-lettered. No stencil: the block hides the fourth side.
visual_arguments.measured: tools/probes/cornered_block_walk.gd, the tower's walker: faces read 1, 2, 3, 1; turned once by a quarter; 3 cm from where it stood after coming in; out by the same door; five corners read 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 1. Desktop only: the headset path (the player body's teleport) is written and not tried.

visual_arguments.title: ONE LAP AND YOUR LEFT IS YOUR RIGHT
visual_arguments.claim: A space can be flat everywhere and still not let you keep your handedness: go round once and the world is mirrored.
visual_arguments.from_the_hall: Not in the hall text. The standing words on this floor already read the wrong way round from behind.
built_from: two cardboard blocks either side of one shared stretch of corridor, the south half the mirror image of the north half
the word LEFT in thick red letters, two skirtings and the door's lettering under one node that is turned over
four wall pieces that open and close the stretch's ends
visual_arguments.what_stands: A cardboard block 4.4 by 7.4 m on the east wing with 'one lap / IN' on its door and a board beside it. STRAIGHT was moved south to make room.
visual_arguments.what_you_do: Go in: LEFT stands on your left. A lap of left turns: it stands on your right and reads backwards, every corner turns right, and the door is shut. A second lap: as it was, and out.
visual_arguments.what_it_shows: A Moebius band's worth of floor: orientation belongs to the way round a space, not to any piece of it. Every triangle in there keeps 180: this is not curvature.
visual_arguments.how: A body cannot be mirrored, so lap two is built as the mirror image of lap one, round a second block. The shared stretch is walked both times and its handed things are turned over while the body is on the far side of a block. The body is never moved. I wrote that this one would need the stencil doorway: it does not - the two sheets are never in view together.
visual_arguments.measured: tools/probes/mirror_lap_walk.gd, the tower's walker: word on the left; after one lap on the right, turned over, the door holds and the old way north is walled; after two as it was, and out by the door (6 of 6).

visual_arguments.title: FIVE SQUARES AT EVERY CORNER
visual_arguments.claim: On a hyperbolic floor a square walk does not close: forward, left, forward, left, forward, left, forward leaves you somewhere else, turned.
visual_arguments.from_the_hall: The bench's DISK and 'The visible rim is infinitely far away in that metric'; the wing's rooms 5 to 7 are travelled by trigger from a deck, this one is walked.
built_from: one round deck whose skin is a shader that draws the tiling round the walker
a pink square of 1.4 m painted on the deck itself, with START
a red pointer at the walker's feet
visual_arguments.what_stands: A deck 5.2 m across south of shaft B, covered in square tiles of which five meet at every corner, crowding toward a dark rim; a board east of it, read from the deck.
visual_arguments.what_you_do: Stand still on START: the tile under you turns red, home. Walk the pink square back to START. Home is 2.4 m away and its arrow has turned 159 degrees; the pointer at your feet shows where it went.
visual_arguments.what_it_shows: The same paces and the same four turns close on the slab and do not close on this floor. With `corner` four the tiles stay where they are and the walk closes; with three (a cube's skin, rounded, six tiles in all) home is 1.2 m away and turned the other way.
visual_arguments.how: The body is never moved. Each step is composed as a motion of the floor (a pair of complex numbers) and the deck's shader folds every fragment into the tile the walker stands in. The arithmetic is the work's own, not the wing's kernel, which has no composition of motions.
visual_arguments.measured: tools/probes/walked_tiling_bench.py (python, before building): a 1.4 m square ends 2.444 m from home turned 158.9 on five, 0 on four, 1.233 m turned -73.1 on three. tools/probes/walked_tiling_walk.gd, the tower's walker: 2.66 m / 168, 0.14 m, 1.31 m / -80 (it stops a hand's width from each corner).

visual_arguments.title: EVERY DOOR, HALF AS FAR
visual_arguments.claim: A rim can be at a finite distance on the picture and infinitely many steps away for the one walking toward it.
visual_arguments.from_the_hall: 'The visible rim is infinitely far away in that metric.'
built_from: a row of stencil doorways, each showing the same corridor at half the size
the rig scaled at each crossing so the corridor always looks full size
visual_arguments.what_stands: A corridor of doors that from outside shrinks to a point three metres away.
visual_arguments.what_you_do: Walk through door after door. From inside every door is as far as the last; from outside you were seen shrinking toward a point you never reached.
visual_arguments.what_it_shows: The Poincare disk's rule for distance, walked along one line.
visual_arguments.needs: scaling the player (XROrigin world scale; the desktop walker has no such thing yet)

open: Plate 6's claim about the disk (no whole surface in the room has its distances) is from memory of Hilbert's theorem and is marked so.
Plate 7's story of Gauss measuring a mountain triangle is unchecked and marked so.

The bench and the hall's film were moved onto the slab by the pass (from [-3, 10] and [4, 11] to [-3.4, 6.4] and [3.2, 8.3]); noneuclidean_wing stood with a column 0.55 m in front of its door and could not be entered; moved to [-9.5, 8].
The hall text does not mention Seven Spaces at all. Plate 8 is the only words on the floor about it besides its own.

One more playable space is written under visual_arguments and not built: the halving door, which needs the player scaled. Three corners and home stands (five by its axis; no five-cornered row is placed), and so do the mirrored lap and the walked tiling. The stencil doorway is proven in the tower's desktop renderer only; the headset's renderer has not been tried.

hanging_board.note: The hall's new stickers on a board with depth, in the sticker app's own medium (laid through its ops by tools/arguments_stickers.ts, drawn in VR by sticker_board, on the web at /stickers?board=arg_noneuclid). Near the cork: what the hall text says. In front: what I made of it.

board.title: Straight: what the hall says, and what I made of it
board.note: An argument's stickers hung in depth: the hall text's own lines near the cork, the reader's lines in front, tied by red thread (commons/data/arguments/NonEuclidean_Spaces.json).

threads.why: The chord is shorter and has left the space: so what changed was what a side may be.
Shorter is only a complaint if I forget which space the corners belong to.
The continuity is the record of three pairs; distances, angles and the sum do not travel with it.
A limit of the picture or the interface is not a limit of the thing shown.
The disk ends on the table; the space it shows has no edge to reach.
The benches bend nothing; and a bend, where there is one, is not yet a rule for distance.
A changed sum is the same record read in another space.
Each reading is precise; which one the world has is a different kind of question.
The record allows three sums; the bench cannot say which the world has.
